headline: High risk: Roo Code’s filesystem, shell, browser, and MCP access can amplify EMQX outputs into unsafe actions or leaks; prompt-injection risk is lower because no direct shared channel is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented between EMQX and Roo Code, so prompt injection is not provably default. However, Roo Code can use MCP, browser, and workspace files, and EMQX can emit HTTP API content; if EMQX output is copied into Roo Code or bridged via files/MCP, instruction hijacking becomes plausible. The pathway is interaction-based, not inherent.
conditions: IF EMQX output is pasted into Roo Code or stored in a workspace file that Roo Code reads, injection becomes possible.
IF an MCP server forwards EMQX content into Roo Code without provenance filtering, Roo Code may follow attacker-controlled instructions.
mitigations: Disable copy/paste of untrusted EMQX output into Roo Code prompts.
Use a separate read-only workspace for EMQX artifacts.
Add a provenance tag to any EMQX-derived file before Roo Code reads it.
Restrict Roo Code MCP servers to trusted, allowlisted endpoints.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization or instruction-stripping before handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress; Roo Code reads and writes workspace files, runs browsers, and can call configured model APIs. If both are used on the same workspace or data path, sensitive IoT data can flow from EMQX into Roo Code context and then out to third-party APIs. The pairwise leakage pathway is plausible in default workflows.
conditions: IF EMQX artifacts containing IoT data are placed in a VS Code workspace that Roo Code reads, leakage risk exists.
IF Roo Code sends workspace contents to a configured model API, EMQX-derived data may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep EMQX data outside Roo Code workspaces.
Use redacted samples instead of raw IoT payloads.
Disable or minimize Roo Code model-context uploads for sensitive files.
Rotate and scope model API keys narrowly.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level data-loss controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX can make broad network calls, while Roo Code can execute shell commands, modify git state, write files, and use MCP. If both operate on the same project or infrastructure, they can race on shared mutable resources and overwrite each other’s changes. Roo Code’s filesystem sharing via workspace makes the conflict default-prone; EMQX’s networked broker role increases blast radius.
conditions: IF EMQX and Roo Code share a writable workspace or repo, concurrent edits can conflict.
IF Roo Code commits or rewrites files while EMQX is serving or generating artifacts, state corruption can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate directories for EMQX and Roo Code.
Pause one agent before the other writes shared files.
Use git branches per agent.
Turn on manual review before any Roo Code commit.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Roo Code can treat workspace content and tool outputs as actionable context, while EMQX can emit HTTP API data and brokered IoT messages. If EMQX output is fed into Roo Code without verification, Roo Code may propagate incorrect facts into code changes, browser actions, or commits. The cascade is plausible, but not directly documented for this pair.
conditions: IF EMQX-generated content is used as Roo Code input without validation, errors can cascade into downstream actions.
IF Roo Code is allowed to commit or execute shell commands based on EMQX-derived text, incorrect outputs can become persistent changes.
mitigations: Require human review of EMQX-derived inputs before Roo Code acts on them.
Use schema validation for any EMQX-to-Roo handoff.
Block direct commit or shell execution from unverified EMQX outputs.
Keep a separate verification step between agents.
requires-engineering: implement typed interfaces for agent handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Roo Code handles source code, browser screenshots, and model-provider API keys. No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented, so compliance risk is limited to overlap and logging practices rather than a proven breach. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined handling of different data classes.
conditions: IF IoT data subject to stricter retention or residency rules is routed into Roo Code logs or model APIs, compliance exposure increases.
IF EMQX data is processed in a jurisdiction or service tier not approved for that data class, policy mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Classify IoT payloads before handoff.
Avoid sending regulated data to Roo Code prompts.
Review model-provider and workspace retention settings.
Store audit logs separately from sensitive content.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention.
